background.definition: Candida species are the most common cause of fungal infections. Systemic candidiasis encompass a wide variety of severe, invasive infections; it is the most common cause of invasive mycosis in the developed world.

list.listitem: A study in an Italian ICU found 16 cases of invasive Candida per 1000 admissions.
Candida species can produce different disorders associated with systemic candidiasis.
More than 17 species have been documented in the literature to cause invasive candidiasis. The most common species include C. albicans, C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis and C. krusei.

Candida albicans is the most common species, but recent studies have shown increase in non-albicans species. An Italian ICU study found that 60% of invasive yeast infections were caused by non-albicans species, most commonly C. parapsilosis.
"High exposure" to antibiotics, especially ciprofloxacin, in critically ill patients may increase the risk of invasive candidal disease.
A history of immunosuppression increases the risk of non-albicans candidemia.
In one series, 8% of endodontic infections involved a candida species.
Increased fungal burden or colonization, typically resulting from use of broad spectrum antimicrobial agents.

Breakdown of normal mucosal and skin barriers as a result of the use of chronic intravascular devices, recent trauma or surgery, and severe mucositis associated with cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiation.
Immune dysfunction(eg neutropnea) that leads to dissemination and proliferation in deep tissue.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Cancer, chemotherapy, and other immunosuppressive therapy
Greater number of organ failures in critically ill patients

list.listitem: Fluconazole IV can be used as prophylaxis in high-risk patients in adult ICUs with a high rate (>5%) of invasive candidiasis. B
Prevention with antifungal medications in critically ill adults does not decrease mortality but may decrease secondary fungal infections. B
Nystatin is no better than placebo in preventing invasive candidiasis in immunocompromised patients and is not recommended. B

While routine ophthalmologic examination has been recommended for all patients with candemia, a systematic review of 38 observational studies with 7472 patients, only 3 potentially benefitted and there was potential for over-investigation and harm.
Blood cultures are useful if positive to identify species and direct therapy. C
1-3 b D glucan test is helpful for the diagnosis (LR+ 5.0, LR− 0.3). C
Germ tube formation test and peptide nucleic acid flourescent in situ hybridization (PNA-FISH) are helpful to differentiate C. albicans species from non albican species. C
Antifungal susceptibility testing is useful in patients who fail therapy and when changing from parenteral to oral therapy. C
Systemic candidiasis can virtually involve any organ, and therefore have a variety of clinical manifestation. There are no distinctive and unique clinical features that are diagnostic.
Manifestations can include but are not limited to fever, rash, dysuria, headache, nausea, vomiting, back pain, and hypotension.
Maintain a high index of suspicion in hospitalized patients, especially in the ICU, who are not responding to antibiotic therapy and in particular those who are immunosuppressed.
A history of immunosuppression increases the risk of non-albicans candidemia.

Blood cultures are useful if positive to identify the candida species, but as many as 50% of blood cultures are negative in patients with proven candidiasis. With new blood cultures technique, sensitivity has improved to 70%.
The 1-3 beta D glucan assay is helpful for the diagnosis with sensitivity of 76% and specificity of 85% (LR+ 5.1, LR− 0.3) in a recent meta-analysis.

Germ tube antibody tests can differentiate albicans from non albicans species. A case-control study, which would tend to overestimate accuracy, found 85% sensitivity and 95% specificity. A systematic review of 7 studies with 976 patients found a somewhat lower accuracy (sensitivity 66%, specificity 76%).
Peptide nucliec acid fluorescent in situ hybridization (PNA-FISH) tests are more rapid than germ tube tests, but are also more expensive and provide modest improvement in sensitivity.
Testing for azole susceptibility is recommended for bloodstream infections and testing for for echinocandin suseptibility should be considered in select patients.
PET/CT (specifically 2 fluorodeoxyglucose PET with CT) may be helpful at monitoring response to therapy, and in a series of 28 patients resulted in a change in management in half.
Suspect systemic candidiasis in hospitalized (especially ICU) patients who fail to respond to antibiotic therapy.
Initial testing should include fungal culture, 1-3 beta D glucan assay, and antibody to candida albicans germ tube.
Consult an infectious disease consultant when the diagnosis is suspected to assist with selection of initial antifungal therapy.

Antifungal therapy should be started as soon as possible with positive blood cultures or high suspicion of candidemia.

Initial therapy can include echinocandin, an azole, amphotericin B, or its derivatives (see ). The choice of treatment depend on clinical status of patient, knowledge of species or antifungal susceptibility, relative drug toxicity, presence of organ dysfunction, available knowledge of the use of the drug in a given patient popultation and patient prior exposure to antifungal agents. Delay in therapy associate with increase morbidity and mortality. Most guidelines including the 2015 IDSA guidelines currently recommend echinocandin as the preferred initial therapy.15,25

Candidemia in non-neutropenic patients: IDSA guidelines recommend an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin) as initial pharmacotherapy for non-neutropenic patients with suspected invasive candidiasis. If susceptibility testing identifies an isolate sensitive to fluconazole, patients should be switched to that drug if stable. Amphotericin B (including the liposomal amphotericin B) is an alternative for patients who do not tolerate the above drugs, or if they are not locally available in poorly resourced settings.

Candidemia in neutropenic patients: an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin) is recommended as initial therapy for patients with neutropenia and suspected invasive candidiasis. Lipid formulation Amphotericin B is effective but has greater potential for toxicity. Fluconazole may be considered as an alternative for selected patients who are not critically ill and have not recently been given an azole drug. Echinocandin is preferred for C. glabrata infections, and fluconazole of liposomal amphotericin B for C. parapsilosis.
A systematic review of 8 studies with a total of 2353 patients comparing amphotericin B wih an echinocandin or voriconazole found no overall difference in efficacy or mortality outcomes.
IDSA guidelines note that while voriconazole is effective for candidemia, it offers no clear advantages over fluconazole.
Patients who are neutropenic at the time of developing candidemia should receive recombinant cytokines to help accelerate the recovery from neutropenia.
Patient with breakthrough or persistance candidemia in the face of ongoing antifungal therapy might have an infected intravascular device, significant immunosuppresion or microbiologic resistance.
For critically ill non-neutropenic patients in the ICU with fever and no other known cause, consider empiric antigungal therapy with an echinocandin.
For patients with prosthetic joint infection due to candida species, two-stage exchange athroplasty or resection arthroplasty may be needed.
Remove central venous catheters from patients with candidemia when they are suspected of being the source.
Antifungal therapy should be continued for 2 weeks after the last positive blood culture and resolution of signs and symptoms of infection.
Parenteral therapy can be switched to oral fluconazole for completion of therapy when patients are clinically stable and once susceptibility testing has been completed.
Crude 30 day mortality is 41%; patients with initial inappropriate therapy can have associated mortality up to 71%. B
Follow up blood culture is recommended to document resolution of infection. C
Ophthalmological examination to rule out retinal involvement is recommended at least once during the course of candidemia. C

IDSA guidelines recommend amphotericin B deoxycholate 1 mg/kg daily for neonates with disseminated candidiasis; fluconazole 12 mg/kg daily is an alternative. Liposomal amphotericin B (3-5 mg/kg daily) is an option if urinary tract involvement can be excluded.

Neonates with positive cultures for candida species should have lumbar puncture and a dilated retinal examination, and if those studies are normal, imaging of the GU tract, liver and spleen to identify a source. Remove (or if necessary, replace) any IV catheters.
Echinocandins should be used with caution and only when amphotericin B and fluconazole are not tolerated or if resistance develops.
There is not enough evidence to compare efficacy of antifungal agents in children.
